title: Astronomers Discover Two 'Super-Puff' Planets Lighter Than Cotton Candy
summary:
Astronomers have discovered a pair of Jupiter-sized exoplanets so light they'd float in a bathtub—if you could find one big enough. Named TOI-791 b and TOI-791 c, these "super-puffs" orbit a Sun-like star about 1,113 light-years from Earth. They're part of a rare class of planets with extremely low density, and finding two in the same system is even rarer.

"Only a handful of these super-puffy planets are known, and it is even rarer to find two in the same system," said Dr. George Dransfield, who led the study. "Their extremely low densities make them fascinating targets for understanding how planetary systems form and evolve."

The first hints came from citizen scientists—volunteers who study NASA's TESS space telescope data. They noticed tiny dips in a star's brightness, which suggested planets were passing in front of it. To confirm, Dransfield's team used telescopes around the world. The ASTEP observatory in Antarctica proved especially useful: the continuous darkness of the Antarctic winter allowed them to record several complete transits. Each transit—when a planet crosses its star and blocks some light—lasted over 11 hours. These were the longest complete planetary transits ever observed from the ground.

By measuring the starlight dips, the team calculated the planets' sizes. They then determined their masses by watching how the planets' gravity tugged on each other's orbits. Together, these measurements revealed incredibly low densities. The two planets also orbit in a rhythmic pattern: for every five orbits the inner planet completes, the outer one completes three. This suggests they formed together from the same disk of gas and dust.

Scientists still aren't sure how super-puffs form. One leading theory is that they have large hydrogen and helium atmospheres around small solid cores, making them appear much larger than they really are. The team hopes to study their atmospheres with the James Webb Space Telescope to solve the mystery. The findings were published in the Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society on June 25, 2026.
why_it_matters: Super-puffs are natural laboratories: because they are so loosely packed, even small changes in their star's radiation can puff them up or strip their atmospheres away, so studying them helps scientists understand how planets form, move, and lose their air — the same kinds of questions that shape how we think about Earth's own atmosphere.

background_read: The first planet found orbiting a Sun-like star was discovered in 1995 (51 Pegasi b), work that later earned its discoverers a Nobel Prize in Physics — before that, scientists could only guess whether planets existed beyond our solar system.

NASA's Kepler space telescope (launched in 2009) found thousands of exoplanets by watching for the same tiny dips in starlight, and TESS (NASA's Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite, launched in 2018) continues that hunt by scanning brighter, nearer stars.
The James Webb Space Telescope (a large infrared observatory launched in 2021) can spread out the light passing through a planet's atmosphere, revealing which gases are present.
A few super-puffs were already known before this discovery, most famously the planets circling the star Kepler-51, whose densities are often compared to cotton candy.
A light-year is the distance light travels in one year — roughly 9.5 trillion kilometres — so 1,113 light-years is unimaginably far away.

perspectives.description: Two super-puffs in one system is a rare find, and the record-breaking 11-hour transits from Antarctica show how much amateurs and unusual locations can contribute to real science.

Only a handful of super-puffs are known, so some scientists warn that the measured sizes and masses could carry big uncertainties — a slightly different size or mass would completely change how strange these planets really are.

The transit method only works when a planet crosses in front of its star from our point of view, which means super-puffs may be more common than we can currently detect, or rarer than the small sample suggests.

The team's next step is using the James Webb Space Telescope to sniff the planets' atmospheres; that data could confirm or wreck the leading 'fluffy hydrogen and helium shell' theory and teach us how planetary systems survive their early, chaotic years.
